title: AI and the impact on the workplace — PCS assistant general secretary John Moloney
pub: Public and Commercial Services Union (PCS) — news/comment, pcs.org.uk
author: John Moloney

dom.t: Worker power: Automation outcomes depend on consultation

mo.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
Worker power: Automation outcomes depend on consultation

kp.k: AI is beginning to affect work and wider society
kp.d: Moloney asserts that AI and associated technologies are beginning to have a substantial impact on work and wider society. The document presents a general workplace perspective rather than a legal-sector analysis and supplies no empirical measurements of that impact.
qs: AI and associated technologies are beginning to have a big impact on the world of work as well as in wider society.

kp.k: AI introduction requires union consultation and agreement
kp.d: PCS advocates making consultation and agreement with the union prerequisites for introducing new AI systems. This is a recommended condition of deployment, not a description of an existing legal requirement.
qs: PCS is clear that new AI systems should only be introduced following consultation and agreement with the union.

kp.k: Job reductions are conditional on enhancing remaining work
kp.d: PCS recognises that AI will affect job roles and conditionally accepts reductions in job numbers only on the understanding that AI enhances rather than degrades jobs. Its stated concern is preventing humans from being reduced to machine-minding roles; it provides no estimate of potential job losses.
qs: While PCS recognises that AI will impact on job roles, we argue it should only be allowed to reduce the number of jobs on the understanding that AI is used to enhance jobs and not to degrade them and therefore prevent humans being reduced to "machine minders".

kp.k: Decisions affecting humans should remain outside AI control
kp.d: Moloney advocates excluding any AI system designed wholly or partly to make decisions affecting humans. The proposed restriction expressly covers recruitment, promotion, transfers and dismissal, and opposes both removing existing human decision-making and automating decisions.
qs: No AI system should be introduced if, in part or whole, it is designed to make any decision that affects humans.
It should not be used to select staff for recruitment, promotion, transfer to another post or dismissal.
It should not remove existing decision making from humans or automate decision making.

kp.k: AI should not manage, evaluate or surveil workers
kp.d: The document extends its proposed restrictions beyond employment selection decisions to allocating, monitoring and evaluating human work, as well as any surveillance of humans. These are normative limits on AI's workplace role rather than findings about observed deployment.
qs: Nor should it be used to allocate, monitor, or evaluate the work of humans or undertake any form of surveillance of humans.

kp.k: Workers should share productivity gains through hours and pay
kp.d: Moloney argues that productivity gains from AI should be shared with workers through reduced hours and increased pay. He frames technology's effects as potentially beneficial or harmful and identifies the benefit of PCS members as the union's objective, without quantifying gains or specifying a distribution formula.
qs: Lastly productivity gains, made through the introduction and use of AI, should be shared with workers in the form of reduced hours and increased pay.
Like all technologies, it can be used for good or bad.
Our aim is that it should be used for the good of PCS members.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Moloney says AI is already beginning to affect work and will change job roles; he sets out PCS's conditions for its introduction rather than predicting particular employment outcomes.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about workplaces, not legal services. Writing as PCS assistant general secretary, John Moloney asserts that AI and associated technologies are beginning to have a large impact on work and wider society. He presents PCS's position that AI should enhance rather than degrade jobs and that any reduction in job numbers should be conditional on that requirement. The possibility of humans becoming 'machine minders' is a risk the union wants to prevent, not a reported outcome. His prohibitions on AI decision-making, recruitment, promotion, transfer, dismissal, work allocation, monitoring, evaluation and surveillance are normative demands, not claims that these uses have already occurred. Likewise, sharing productivity gains through shorter hours and higher pay is a proposed distributional policy, not a forecast.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source offers a union policy position and general assertions, without empirical support or specific examples.
pts.d: Moloney speaks in his capacity as PCS assistant general secretary and attributes the policy positions to PCS. The document provides no data, benchmarks, workplace cases, quantified productivity estimates, job-loss figures or explicit experiential evidence for its claims about existing impact or future changes to job roles. The institutional position supplies the perspective, not a measured evidential basis.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Impact is described as beginning at the time of the 2024 commentary; future changes have no specified horizon and are subject to proposed union safeguards.
pts.d: The statement that impact is 'beginning' concerns the source's present, while changes to job roles are prospective without a date, pace or magnitude. PCS calls for consultation and union agreement before introduction. Its stated conditions include enhancing rather than degrading jobs, retaining human decision-making, excluding AI from decisions affecting humans and from managing or surveilling their work, and sharing any resulting productivity gains with workers. These are desired conditions for adoption, not conditions empirically shown to determine AI's effects.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Workers, especially PCS members, are the central affected group, with broader concern for anyone subject to AI decisions.
pts.d: Moloney identifies potential changes to workers' job roles, job numbers, job quality and decision-making responsibility. His safeguards address people subject to recruitment, promotion, transfer or dismissal decisions and workers exposed to automated allocation, monitoring, evaluation or surveillance. Workers are the intended beneficiaries of shorter hours and increased pay from productivity gains; PCS members are the expressly named constituency. The opening also refers to wider society, but does not specify particular societal outcomes or make claims about lawyers, law firms or legal clients.
